'''''Polytrichastrum formosum''''', commonly known as the '''bank haircap moss''',<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Webmaster |first=David Ratz |title=Bank Haircap Moss - Montana Field Guide |url=https://fieldguide.mt.gov/speciesDetail.aspx?elcode=NBMUS5T020 |access-date=2022-04-05 |website=fieldguide.mt.gov |language=en}}</ref> is a species of [[moss]] belonging to the family [[Polytrichaceae]].

It has a [[cosmopolitan distribution]], found mostly in temperate latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Flora of North America North of Mexico |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065248 |title=Bryophyta: Mosses, part 1 |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2007 |isbn=9780195318234 |volume=27 |location=New York |pages=130}}</ref> and especially dominant in Europe and North America. However, it has also been identified in India, China, Nepal, Japan, Algeria, Australia, New Zealand, Russia, Turkey, Syria, and the Atlantic islands (i.e. Iceland).<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Asthana |first1=Ashish Kumar |last2=Vinay |first2=Sahu |last3=Nath |first3=Virendra |date=2012 |title=''Polytrichastrum formosum''(Hedw.) G.L. Smith in India |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.7872/cryb.v33.iss1.2012.087 |journal=Cryptogamie, Bryologie |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=87–90 |doi=10.7872/cryb.v33.iss1.2012.087 |s2cid=85607035 |issn=1290-0796|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite book |title=Atlas of British & Irish bryophytes : the distribution and habitat of mosses and liverworts in Britain and Ireland |date=2014 |others=T. L. Blockeel, Sam D. S. Bosanquet, M. O. Hill, C. D. Preston, British Bryological Society |isbn=978-1-874357-62-9 |location=Newbury, Berkshire |pages=418 |chapter=Polytrichastrum formosum |oclc=898120353}}</ref>

This species was previously called ''Polytrichum formosum'' but has been reclassified as ''Polytrichastrum formosum'' due to distinct sporangial features.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=Merrill |first=G. L. Smith |date=1992 |title=Notes on North American Polytrichaceae: Polytrichastrum |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3243483 |journal=The Bryologist |volume=95 |issue=3 |pages=270–273 |doi=10.2307/3243483 |jstor=3243483 |issn=0007-2745|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Recent molecular studies suggest that it should be moved back to its original genus (''Polytrichum''),<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=Neil E. |last2=Hyvönen |first2=Jaakko |date=2010a |title=A phylogenetic circumscription of Polytrichastrum (Polytrichaceae): Reassessment of sporophyte morphology supports molecular phylogeny |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.3732/ajb.0900161 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=97 |issue=4 |pages=566–578 |doi=10.3732/ajb.0900161|pmid=21622419 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> however [[Bryology|bryologists]] have not yet reached a consensus.  

== Habitat ==
''Polytrichastrum formosum'' generally inhabits shaded, poor soils and humus in damp coniferous forests and cool temperate rainforests.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=Neil |last2=Kariyawasam |first2=Isuru |last3=Flores |first3=Jorge |last4=Hyvönen |first4=Jaakko |date=2021-06-30 |title=The diversity of the Polytrichopsida—a review |url=https://www.mapress.com/bde/article/view/bde.43.1.8 |journal=Bryophyte Diversity and Evolution |volume=43 |issue=1 |doi=10.11646/bde.43.1.8 |s2cid=237385196 |issn=2381-9685|doi-access=free }}</ref> This species is most common in Europe and grows in grasslands, lowland heaths, acidic moorlands, rocky slopes, and old buildings.<ref name=":8" />

== Gametophyte ==
Like all moss, the [[haploid]] [[gametophyte]] is the dominant phase of the lifecycle of ''P. formosum.'' The moss gametophyte has photosynthetic leaves, a stem, and root-like rhizoids that anchor them to the substrate.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Glime |first=J. M. |url=http://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/bryophyte-ecology/ |title=Bryophyte Ecology. Volume 1. Physiological Ecology. |publisher=Michigan Technological University and the International Association of Bryologists. |year=2017 |chapter=Meet the Bryophytes. Chapt. 2-1}}</ref>

''Polytrichastrum formosum'' is a medium to large robust acrocarpous moss, growing in uncrowded, unbranching tufts.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":7" /> Its colour ranges from green to dark olive green to greenish black. The stems of mature plants are generally 3 to 8 cm tall, however they can be as short as 2 cm or as tall as 20 cm.<ref name=":7" /> ''P. formosum'', like all members of Polytrichaceae, is an endohydric moss, meaning water conduction occurs internally.<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last=Glime |first=J.M. |url=http://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/bryophyte-ecology/ |title=Bryophyte Ecology. Volume 1. Physiological Ecology |publisher=Michigan Technological University and the International Association of Bryologists |year=2017 |chapter=Water Relations: Conducting Structures. Chapt. 7-1}}</ref> This process is made possible by a central conducting strand in the stem, made up of hydroids, which are cells specialized for water transport.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Glime |first=J.M. |url=http://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/bryophyte-ecology/ |title=Bryophyte Ecology. Volume 1. Physiological Ecology |publisher=Michigan Technological University and the International Association of Bryologists |year=2017 |chapter=Bryophyta - Andreaeopsida, Andreaeobryopsida, Polytrichopsida. Chapt. 2-6.}}</ref><ref name=":42">{{Cite journal |last1=PRESSEL |first1=SILVIA |last2=LIGRONE |first2=ROBERTO |last3=DUCKETT |first3=JEFFREY G. |date=2006 |title=Effects of De- and Rehydration on Food-conducting Cells in the Moss Polytrichum formosum: A Cytological Study |journal=Annals of Botany |volume=98 |issue=1 |pages=67–76 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcl092 |issn=0305-7364 |pmc=2803544 |pmid=16735407}}</ref> The stem also contains leptoids and specialized parenchyma cells that are used for conducting sugars throughout the plant.<ref name=":42" /> The hydrome (made of hydroids) and leptome (made of leptoids) are considered analogous in function to [[xylem]] and [[phloem]] in vascular plants.<ref name=":32" /> For structural support there are also thick-walled stereid cells circling the hydrome, which helps the moss grow tall.<ref name=":32" />
[[File:Polytrichum_formosum_(k,_144735-474752)_6720.JPG|left|thumb|280x280px|Ventral surface of a leaf from ''P. formosum.'']]
The leaves of ''Polytrichastrum formosum'' are [[Glossary of leaf morphology|linear-lanceolate]], and are usually 6 to 8 mm in length, but can be up to 12 mm long.<ref name=":7" /> They are erect to spreading when the moss is dry but become broadly recurved when moist.<ref name=":7" /> The leaves have a toothed margin and a prominent costa, where guide cells help conduct water throughout the leaf, and stereids on the dorsal side provide protection.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Proctor |first1=Michael C. F. |last2=Ligrone |first2=Roberto |last3=Duckett |first3=Jeffrey G. |date=2007-01-01 |title=Desiccation Tolerance in the Moss Polytrichum formosum: Physiological and Fine-structural Changes during Desiccation and Recovery |journal=Annals of Botany |language=en |volume=99 |issue=1 |pages=75–93 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcl246 |issn=0305-7364 |pmc=2802982 |pmid=17158142}}</ref>
[[File:Polytrichastrum_formosum_(g,_144932-481517)_3305.JPG|thumb|287x287px|Cross-section of ''P. formosum'' leaf, revealing photosynthetic lamellae.]]

Using a microscope, photosynthetic [[Lamella (cell biology)|lamellae]] are visible in cross section, nearly covering the entire ventral surface of the leaf.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":7" /> A feature unique to Polytrichaceae, lamellae are often compared to the [[Leaf|mesophyll]] of vascular plants due to their role in photosynthesis.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=Robert J. |last2=Ryder |first2=Steve H. |last3=Gardner |first3=Mark I. |last4=Sheetz |first4=Jonathan P. |last5=Nichipor |first5=Stephen D. |date=1996 |title=Photosynthetic Function of Leaf Lamellae in Polytrichum commune |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3244431 |journal=The Bryologist |volume=99 |issue=1 |pages=6–11 |doi=10.2307/3244431 |jstor=3244431 |issn=0007-2745|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Each lamella stands 3 to 7 cells high and the cells at the top are smooth and oblong.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":7" /> Lamellae help increase desiccation tolerance and photosynthetic efficiency by providing more surface area for light absorption and gas exchange.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Proctor |first=M. C. F. |date=2005 |title=Why do Polytrichaceae have lamellae? |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/174328205X69968 |journal=Journal of Bryology |language=en |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=221–229 |doi=10.1179/174328205X69968 |bibcode=2005JBryo..27..221P |s2cid=84580845 |issn=0373-6687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The lamellae are covered by a layer of hydrophobic wax that protects the air spaces between neighbouring lamella from being flooded with water, which would impede CO<sub>2</sub> uptake necessary for photosynthesis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clayton-Greene |first1=K. A. |last2=Collins |first2=N. J. |last3=Green |first3=T. G. A. |last4=Proctor |first4=M. C. F. |date=1985-01-01 |title=Surface wax, structure and function in leaves of Polytrichaceae |url=https://doi.org/10.1179/jbr.1985.13.4.549 |journal=Journal of Bryology |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=549–562 |doi=10.1179/jbr.1985.13.4.549 |bibcode=1985JBryo..13..549C |issn=0373-6687|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":6" /> In this way, ''P. formosum'' is able withstand high irradiance better than other mosses.

== Sporophyte ==
[[File:Polytrichastrum_formosum_(a,_145137-481315)_6354.jpg|thumb|''P. formosum'' angled sporophyte capsules (calyptra absent).]]
The [[diploid]] [[sporophyte]] generation of ''P. formosum'' matures in early summer and is short-lived.<ref name=":8" /> The solitary sporophyte grows out of the female gametophyte, relying on it for energy and nutrients. It is anchored to the gametophyte by a foot, and has a stalk (seta) elevating a capsule ([[Sporangium|sporangia]]) in which spores will develop via [[meiosis]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Glime |first=J. M. |url=http://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/bryophyte-ecology/ |title=Bryophyte Ecology. Volume 1. Physiological Ecology. |publisher=Michigan Technological University and the International Association of Bryologists |year=2017 |chapter=Ecophysiology of Development: Sporophyte. Chapt. 5-9.}}</ref> The seta is yellowish to reddish brown and is 3 to 6 cm tall.<ref name=":7" /> Like the stem of the gametophyte, the seta has a hydrome and leptome for conducting water and sugars from the gametophyte.<ref name=":3" /> The slender and short-rectangular capsule is ochre to brown and 4 to 7 mm long.<ref name=":7" /> The capsule is [[terete]] or 4-6 angled, which distinguishes ''Polytrichastrum'' species from ''Polytrichum'' species.<ref name=":9" /> In the early stages of growth the capsule is covered by a hairy calyptra that protects the capsule during development and influences it's shape. At maturity, the calyptra falls off to reveal a beaked operculum.<ref name=":3" /> Like most other moss in Polytrichaceae, under the operculum ''P. formosom'' has 64 nematodontous peristome teeth that surround an epiphragm.<ref name=":0" />

== Reproduction ==

=== Sexual reproduction ===
''Polytrichastrum formosum'' is sexually [[Dioicy|dioicous]], meaning the male and female reproductive structures are on separate plants.<ref name=":7" /> ''P. formosum,'' like all members of the Polytrichaceae family, is an acrocarpous or cushion moss with reproductive structures borne at the terminus of the gametophyte stem. The perichaetial leaves surrounding the [[Archegonium|archegonia]] (female reproductive structure) resembles the other stem leaves besides being longer.<ref name=":7" /> The [[Antheridium|antheridia]] (male reproductive structure) are at the apex of the male gametophyte in a cup-like structure formed by perigonial leaves which are modified stem leaves.<ref name=":4" /> Sperm is produced in the antheridia via [[mitosis]], and when mature they are released from the antheridia by raindrops splashing onto the cup. Sperm can be dispersed up to one meter from the male, and if they successfully reach an archegonia, the egg will be fertilized and grow into a diploid sporophyte.<ref name=":4" />

=== Asexual reproduction ===
Asexual reproduction is not extensive in ''P. formosum'', however it occurs on a local scale by the vegetative proliferation of [[Genet (biology)|genets]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van der Velde |first1=M. |last2=During |first2=H. J. |last3=Van de Zande |first3=L. |last4=Bijlsma |first4=R. |date=2001-12-21 |title=The reproductive biology of Polytrichum formosum: clonal structure and paternity revealed by microsatellites: REPRODUCTIVE BIOLOGY OF POLYTRICHUM FORMOSUM |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1046/j.0962-1083.2001.01385.x |journal=Molecular Ecology |language=en |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=2423–2434 |doi=10.1046/j.0962-1083.2001.01385.x|pmid=11742546 |s2cid=19716812 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Taxonomy disagreement ===
When this species was first described by [[Johann Hedwig]] in 1801, it was classified as ''Polytrichum formosum.''<ref name=":11" /> Upon further analysis it was determined by Gary L. Smith in 1971 that the moss is better described by the ''Polytrichastrum'' genus.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last=Smith |first=Gary L. |date=1971 |title=A conspectus of the genera of Polytrichaceae |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065248 |journal=Mem. New York Bot. Gard. |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=1–83 |isbn=978-0893270728}}</ref> ''Polytrichastrum'' can be distinguished from ''Polytrichum'' by sporangial features including multiple-angled capsules (more than 4 sided), elongated peristome teeth surrounding the ridged epiphragm, and larger spores.<ref name=":9" /> According to several sources, ''Polytrichastrum formosum'' remains the most accurate taxonomic classification.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=ITIS - Report: Polytrichastrum formosum |url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=549026#null |access-date=2022-04-13 |website=www.itis.gov}}</ref> However, more recent molecular data and phylogenetic analysis suggests that ''P. formosum'' should be reverted to its original genus: ''Polytrichum''.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":0" /> Their study suggested that species in ''Polytrichastrum'' and ''Polytrichum'' are in fact distantly related, but because the ''Polytrichastrum'' genus is [[Polyphyly|polyphyletic]], authors suggested that some species, including ''P. formosum,'' return to the ''Polytrichum'' genus.<ref name=":10" /> Currently, these names remain synonyms.
